intro: Everyone talks about food: what we eat, when we eat and what we like. This lesson gives you the key words and the common traps: “have breakfast”, uncountable words like “bread”, and confusing words (raisins, chips).
objectifs: Name the meals and say what you eat with “have breakfast / lunch / dinner”.
Know the most common foods and drinks.
Count uncountable food with a glass of, a piece of, a cup of…
Talk about what you like and describe a dish (delicious, spicy, sweet).

texte: The three meals are “breakfast” (morning), “lunch” (midday) and “dinner” (evening). A little food between meals is “a snack”.
To say you eat a meal, use “have”, not “take”: “I have breakfast at seven.” Don't use an article before the meal: “have lunch”, not “have the lunch”.
To say what you eat at a meal, use “for”: “What do you have for breakfast? — I have bread and tea.”
exemples: I have breakfast at half past six.
have + meal, no article.
What do you have for lunch? — Usually rice and fish.
for + meal.
We have dinner with the family on Sundays.
A habit: present simple.
sections.note: In Britain, the evening meal is also called “tea” (in the north) or “supper” (a light, late meal). In the USA, “dinner” is always the evening meal.

texte: Here are the most useful words in groups. Many foods (rice, bread, meat, cheese, water) are uncountable: they have no plural and don't take “a”.

lignes: an apple · a banana · an orange · a mango · a pineapple · grapes
a tomato · a potato · an onion · a carrot · beans · salad
water · tea · coffee · juice · soft drinks

exemples: I eat a lot of fruit and vegetables.
“fruit” is usually singular in general.
Do you want chicken or fish?
No article: uncountable meat.

texte: Some foods are countable: an apple, two apples, an egg. Others are uncountable: bread, rice, water, milk, meat, cheese, sugar. Don't say “a bread” or “two waters” (but in a café, “two coffees” means two cups of coffee).
To talk in general, use the noun alone: “I like bread.” For an amount that is not exact, use “some” (lesson 31): “I'd like some water.”
To count, add a quantity word or a container: a glass of water, a piece of bread. Lessons 30 and 31 look at this in more detail.

lignes: a glass of water / milk / juice
a piece of bread / cake / cheese

exemples: Can I have a glass of water, please?
A polite request.
I eat two slices of bread for breakfast.
The quantity word takes the plural: slices.

sections.titre: Saying what you like and describing a dish
texte: Your tastes: “I like fish”, “I don't like coffee”, “My favourite food is ndolé”. Your diet: “I'm vegetarian” (I don't eat meat), “I don't eat pork”.
To describe a dish: delicious, tasty (with a good taste), spicy / hot (with a lot of chilli), sweet (with sugar), salty (with salt), fresh (new, not old).
Careful: “cook” is a verb (to make food) and a noun (a person who cooks). “A cooker” is a machine in the kitchen (US: a stove), not a person!
exemples: This soup is delicious!
A very good taste.
Be careful, the sauce is very spicy.
A lot of chilli.
My father is a great cook.
cook = a person.

texte: Some words look like words in other languages but have a different meaning, and some change between British and American English.

lignes: US: fries; thin dry ones: crisps (UK), chips (US)

formule: have breakfast / lunch / dinner · What do you have for breakfast? · a glass of water, a piece of bread
prononciation: Don't mix up “chicken” /ˈtʃɪkɪn/ (the bird, the meat) and “kitchen” /ˈkɪtʃɪn/ (the room): the “ch” sound moves.
“dessert” /dɪˈzɜːt/ has the stress at the end; “desert” /ˈdezət/ has the stress at the start.
“bread” /bred/ and “fruit” /fruːt/: you hear only one vowel; the i in “fruit” is silent.
erreurs: I take my breakfast at 7.
I have breakfast at 7.
For a meal: “have”, with no article.
Can I have a bread?
Can I have some bread? / Can I have a piece of bread?
“Bread” is uncountable.
I eat a rice every day.
I eat rice every day.
No “a” before an uncountable noun.
I love raisins, especially fresh ones.
I love grapes.
Fresh = grapes; dried = raisins.
My mother is a good cooker.
My mother is a good cook.
“Cooker” = the machine for cooking.
We have the lunch at noon.
We have lunch at noon.
No article before breakfast, lunch, dinner.
I eat many fruits.
I eat a lot of fruit.
In general, “fruit” is used as an uncountable noun.
I'd like a cup of tea with a milk.
I'd like a cup of tea with milk.
“Milk” is uncountable: no “a”.

dialogue.contexte: In Douala, two colleagues, Brice and Hannah (from Canada), choose a restaurant for lunch.
lignes: It's one o'clock. Let's have lunch!
Good idea. I'm hungry. What do people eat here for lunch?
Try ndolé. It's a dish with leaves, peanuts and meat or fish.
Not very. And you can have it with plantain or rice.
Perfect. I love plantain. And to drink?
A bottle of water for me, and a fresh juice for you?
Yes, please. Mango juice! This is a delicious lunch.
“a delicious lunch”: article because of the adjective.

mots: the first meal of the day
the meal in the middle of the day
the main meal in the evening
I have a snack at four o'clock.
a plant we eat, like a carrot or an onion
food from animals, like beef or chicken
small white or brown grains that we cook
My brother is a good cook.
to make food; a person who makes food

exercices.consigne: Give the name of the meal.
items: The meal in the middle of the day
The main meal in the evening

exercices.consigne: Complete with glass, cup, piece, bowl, bottle or bar.

items: She drinks ___ water with her meals.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I take breakfast at eight o'clock.
I have breakfast at eight o'clock.
I'd like a glass of water, please. / I'd like some water, please.
My brother is a very good cooker.
My brother is a very good cook.
What do you have at lunch?
What do you have for lunch?

exercices.consigne: Describe your meals on a normal day in four or five sentences: what you eat and drink, and when. Say what your favourite food is.
items: I have breakfast at seven: two slices of bread with butter and a cup of coffee. For lunch I usually have rice and chicken. At four o'clock I have a snack, often a banana. I have dinner at eight with my family. My favourite food is grilled fish with plantain.

a_retenir: have breakfast / lunch / dinner (not take, no article); What do you have for lunch?
bread, rice, water, milk, meat, cheese: uncountable, no “a”, no plural.
To count: a glass of, a cup of, a bottle of, a piece of, a slice of, a bowl of.
Careful: grapes (fresh) vs raisins (dried); chips (UK) = fries (US); a cook = a person, a cooker = a machine.
To describe a dish: delicious, tasty, spicy, sweet, salty, fresh.
